title: Scaling Kafka: from one broker to mirrored regional clusters
caption: Each stage removes the bottleneck of the previous one; switch the 📈 tabs to grow the system.

steps.text: One broker holds every topic with a single copy. Easy to run, and plenty for a pilot at one airport.
But a dead disk loses records, and a restart stops every producer and consumer: a single point of failure for the whole operation.

scenarios.name: v2: 3 brokers, RF=3
scenarios.summary: Three brokers each hold a copy of every partition, and leaders are spread across them, so one broker can fail without losing data or stopping writes.

steps.text: Every partition has 3 replicas on 3 brokers, with the leaders spread, so writes are spread too.
Followers pull each partition from its leader. acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2: a broker can die, or be patched, without losing an acknowledged record or stopping writes.
Cost: 3× the disk and replication traffic, and a few ms more per write. The next limit is a consumer group's parallelism, capped by the partition count.

scenarios.name: v3: more partitions
scenarios.summary: Raise flight-status from 24 to 64 partitions on 6 brokers so the groups that fall behind in a storm can grow past 24 members.

steps.text: A group can have at most one active member per partition. At 24 partitions, notifications stopped scaling at 24 members in the last storm.
With 64 partitions on 6 brokers, the busy groups grow when they need to, and the quiet ones (display boards) stay small.

Cost: hash(key) mod N changes, so a leg's new events land on a different partition than its old ones. bookings must be repartitioned at the same time to keep the join co-partitioned. Size for peak once, and expect more open files and slower failovers per broker.

scenarios.name: v4: regional clusters
scenarios.summary: One cluster per region keeps writes local and a regional outage contained; mirroring copies the topics the other region needs.

steps.text: Each region's flight ops writes to its own cluster: low latency, and a regional outage stays regional.
A mirror in each destination region copies the topics it needs under a prefixed name (eu.flight-status), so records never loop back. A US gate agent sees an inbound EU flight's delay.

Cost: mirroring is asynchronous (seconds behind), and offsets differ between clusters, so a consumer that fails over needs translated offsets (mirror checkpoints) and idempotent handling of the overlap.
